clue.text: She span fabric round

parts.note: fabric is cloth, material woven on a loom
a round shape is a ring, the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone spun some material into a circle.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth the three Fates are Clotho, Lachesis and Atropos; Clotho spins the thread of each human life. 'span' is the old past tense of 'spin'.
explanation.definitionFit: Of the three Fates of Greek myth, she is the spinner who draws out the thread of life.

clue.text: His emblems to be found in 10

definitions.text: His emblems to be found in 10

parts.words: His emblems to be found in 10
parts.note: entry 10 is a temple of the Persian god Mithras, so these are Mithraic Emblems, a 1936 poetry collection by a South African poet

explanation.surface: A man's badges are kept in a particular place.
explanation.walkthrough: Roy Campbell, the South African poet, published Mithraic Emblems; 10 across is a MITHRAEUM, so 'emblems in 10' are Mithraic ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Roy Campbell wrote the poetry collection Mithraic Emblems, linking him to the Mithras temple at 10.

clue.text: Some choices by Porter

definitions.meaning: William Sydney Porter, writing as O. Henry, published a 1909 story collection under this title

explanation.definitionFit: The plural means alternatives to choose from, and it is also the title of an O. Henry story collection; Porter was his real surname.

clue.text: Like some tasks assigned to Poirot?

definitions.text: Like some tasks assigned to Poirot?

parts.words: Like some tasks assigned to Poirot?
parts.note: Agatha Christie's The Labours of Hercules gives her Belgian detective twelve cases echoing the hero's mythical labours

explanation.surface: A question about the jobs given to Agatha Christie's detective.
explanation.walkthrough: Hercule Poirot shares his first name with the Greek hero, and Christie's collection The Labours of Hercules sets him twelve matching cases.
explanation.definitionFit: Enormously demanding tasks are described with an adjective from the Greek strongman's twelve labours, and Poirot's own name is Hercule.

clue.text: Hero badly let by a bit of a heel

definitions.text: Hero badly let by a bit of a heel

parts.words: Hero badly let by a bit of a heel
parts.note: the Greek warrior at Troy was invulnerable except at one spot, where his mother held him when dipping him in the Styx, and an arrow there killed him

explanation.surface: A champion was let down by a scoundrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heel' looks like a cad who betrayed the hero; in fact it is the literal heel, the one vulnerable part of the Greek hero, struck by Paris's arrow.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek warrior of the Iliad died from a wound to his heel, the only unprotected part of his body.

clue.text: Body of work perhaps inevitably including lost illusions

definitions.text: Body of work perhaps inevitably including lost illusions

parts.words: Body of work perhaps inevitably including lost illusions
parts.note: Balzac's vast cycle of interlinked novels includes Illusions perdues, translated Lost Illusions

explanation.surface: Any large output of work will contain some disappointments.
explanation.walkthrough: Balzac grouped nearly a hundred novels and stories under one title, La Comédie humaine; one of them is Illusions perdues (Lost Illusions).
explanation.definitionFit: Balzac's collected fiction, his whole body of work, is known by this French title, and it contains the novel Lost Illusions.

clue.text: Dostoevsky's mature version of Wordsworth's boy?

definitions.text: Dostoevsky's mature version of Wordsworth's boy?

parts.words: Dostoevsky's mature version of Wordsworth's boy?
parts.note: Wordsworth wrote a ballad about a simple-minded boy, and Dostoevsky wrote a novel about a grown man, Prince Myshkin, called by the same word

explanation.surface: Was the Russian novelist's hero a grown-up form of the poet's lad?
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's ballad is The Idiot Boy; Dostoevsky's novel is The Idiot, so his is the adult version.
explanation.definitionFit: Dostoevsky's novel and Wordsworth's ballad share the word for a simpleton in their titles, one about a man, one about a boy.

clue.text: He of 14 offers the French story

parts.note: le is the French masculine word for 'the'
conte is French for a tale or short story

explanation.surface: A Frenchman tells a tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 14 across is LISLE, and the nineteenth-century poet Leconte de Lisle is 'he of Lisle'; 'offers' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: The French Parnassian poet Charles Marie Leconte de Lisle carries the name at 14 as his territorial suffix.

clue.text: That of Inferno expounded by Jones

definitions.text: That of Inferno expounded by Jones

parts.words: That of Inferno expounded by Jones
parts.note: LeRoi Jones, later Amiri Baraka

explanation.surface: Someone called Jones explains the structure of Dante's hell.
explanation.walkthrough: Inferno is the first part of Dante's Divine Comedy, set in Hell, so Jones's book title fits.
explanation.definitionFit: An organised scheme or structure; LeRoi Jones's novel is The System of Dante's Hell, Dante's Inferno.

clue.text: Lowry man, not matchstick, but offering my fire, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of the phrase could be put another way, rearranged

parts.note: the fodder letters, taken as written

explanation.surface: A man painted by Lowry is not one of his stick figures but someone offering a light.
explanation.walkthrough: L. S. Lowry, the English painter, is famous for 'matchstick men'; the other Lowry is Malcolm, whose Under the Volcano has the consul as hero. 'perhaps' rearranges OFFERING MY FIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Malcolm Lowry's novel Under the Volcano centres on the alcoholic British consul of that name.

clue.text: Their mum a stranger in temple of Persian god

indicators.note: stranger read as 'more strange', so the letters are made odder by being rearranged

explanation.surface: Their mother seems out of place in a temple of a Persian deity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stranger' looks like a noun, a newcomer; it is the comparative adjective telling you to rearrange THEIR MUM A.
explanation.definitionFit: Mithras was a Persian god whose Roman cult met in underground shrines, each one called by this name.

clue.text: People discovered in Spain (Castile)

indicators.note: discovered means found inside the words that follow, so the letters lie within them

explanation.surface: A nation found in a Spanish region.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Spanish conquerors discovering a people; the Inca empire was indeed conquered by Castile's Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: A South American people whose empire in the Andes was overthrown by Spanish conquistadors.

clue.text: Victor in very early submarine battle

definitions.text: Victor in very early submarine battle

parts.words: Victor in very early submarine battle
parts.note: in the Old English epic the hero dives to the bottom of a mere and kills Grendel's mother in an underwater fight

explanation.surface: Someone who won one of the first undersea naval engagements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'submarine battle' suggests warships, but it means a fight literally under the sea: the Old English hero kills Grendel's mother beneath the lake.
explanation.definitionFit: The hero of the Old English epic defeats Grendel's mother in a fight under the waters of a mere.

clue.text: Thriller writer made ten (ten!) errors, including relaxing of tension

annotationWithheld.why: Thriller writer made ten (ten!) errors, including relaxing of tension (7): DETENTE is defined by 'relaxing of tension', but no reading of the rest gives its letters; 'made ten ten' rearranged leaves M, A, N over with no clue word for them
annotationWithheld.clue: Thriller writer made ten (ten!) errors, including relaxing of tension

clue.text: Rumoured sea-girt provenance of anthem composer

indicators.note: rumoured means heard said by others, so the word is judged by its sound

parts.note: sea-girt means ringed by sea, an island, so coming from one is French 'de l'île', of the isle, said 'leel'

explanation.surface: A national anthem's composer reportedly came from an island.
explanation.walkthrough: Claude Joseph Rouget de Lisle wrote La Marseillaise; 'de Lisle' sounds like French 'de l'isle', from the island.
explanation.definitionFit: Rouget de Lisle composed La Marseillaise, the French national anthem, in 1792.

clue.text: "In this chamber —- —— Vivaldi, in a voice of desperation" (Ann Radcliffe)

definitions.text: "In this chamber —- —— Vivaldi, in a voice of desperation" (Ann Radcliffe)

parts.words: "In this chamber —- —— Vivaldi, in a voice of desperation" (Ann Radcliffe)
parts.note: a gap-fill quotation from Radcliffe's Gothic novel The Italian, whose hero is Vincentio di Vivaldi; the missing hyphenated verb means sounded again

explanation.surface: A line from a Gothic novel with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Vivaldi here is the hero of Radcliffe's The Italian, not the composer; the blank is filled by a verb for a voice repeated by the walls of the room.
explanation.definitionFit: Resounded or reverberated, as a cry repeated by the walls of a vault.

clue.text: Beckett character at ancient city is at first a basic interest for king of antiquity

parts.note: Hamm is the blind master in Samuel Beckett's play Endgame
Ur is the ancient Sumerian city in Mesopotamia

indicators.note: at first asks for the opening letter of each of the next three words

explanation.surface: A character from Beckett, set in an ancient city, has a basic interest in an old king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at' and 'is' just link the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The Babylonian ruler of the eighteenth century BC known for his law code.

clue.text: The radio play … competing with Soviet art-cinema rather than with Hollywood or the standardized 1-—"(Louis MacNeice, Christopher Columbus)

definitions.text: The radio play … competing with Soviet art-cinema rather than with Hollywood or the standardized 1-—"(Louis MacNeice, Christopher Columbus)

parts.words: The radio play … competing with Soviet art-cinema rather than with Hollywood or the standardized 1-—"(Louis MacNeice, Christopher Columbus)
parts.note: a gap-fill quotation from MacNeice's introduction to his radio play; the blank is the short film of current events shown in cinemas

explanation.surface: A quoted passage about how a radio play should rival Soviet art films.
explanation.walkthrough: The blank is a hyphenated name for the topical short film that preceded features in cinemas of the 1930s and 1940s.
explanation.definitionFit: A short cinema film of current affairs, shown before the main feature in the mid-twentieth century.

clue.text: Bertie's titular gratitude to the help

definitions.text: Bertie's titular gratitude to the help

parts.words: Bertie's titular gratitude to the help
parts.note: P. G. Wodehouse's novel with Bertie Wooster thanking his valet is titled with those words followed by the valet's name

explanation.surface: Bertie, in a book title, thanks his servant.
explanation.walkthrough: Wodehouse's 1934 novel is Thank You, Jeeves; 'the help' means a servant, here the valet Jeeves.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase of gratitude that opens Wodehouse's title addressed to Bertie Wooster's valet.

clue.text: Source of characters of Shakespeare's plays

definitions.text: Source of characters of Shakespeare's plays

parts.words: Source of characters of Shakespeare's plays
parts.note: the Romantic essayist wrote a critical book titled Characters of Shakespear's Plays in 1817

explanation.surface: Where the people in Shakespeare's dramas came from.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a question about Shakespeare's sources, but it names the essayist William Hazlitt, author of Characters of Shakespear's Plays.
explanation.definitionFit: The English essayist William Hazlitt wrote the 1817 critical study with that title.

clue.text: Came together concerning disposition of feet

parts.note: people who came together met
re is a Latin-derived word meaning about or concerning

explanation.surface: People gathered about how to arrange their feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'feet' are the units of verse, not body parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Poetic rhythm is the arrangement of stressed and unstressed syllables in feet.

clue.text: Henri offered it at noon

parts.note: the Liverpool poet Adrian Henri wrote a poem whose title pairs this evening word with 'at Noon'

explanation.surface: A Frenchman made an offer at midday.
explanation.walkthrough: Henri is not a Frenchman but Adrian Henri, one of the Liverpool poets; his poem is 'Tonight at Noon'.
explanation.definitionFit: This evening, the opening word of Adrian Henri's paradoxical poem title ending 'at Noon'.

clue.text: Mrs Y anyhow not applicable in one of seven ancient churches

indicators.note: anyhow means in any old way, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: N/A is the usual form abbreviation for not applicable

explanation.surface: A woman called Mrs Y is unsuitable in a church.
explanation.definitionFit: The Book of Revelation addresses seven churches of Asia, one at this port city, now Izmir in Turkey.

clue.text: Young Italian charcoal burner

definitions.meaning: a founder of Young Italy, the 1831 patriotic movement
a member of the Carbonari, the secret society whose name means charcoal burners

explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Mazzini founded the Young Italy movement and had earlier joined the Carbonari, the 'charcoal burners'.

clue.text: Brand loyalty is expected of his admirers

definitions.text: Brand loyalty is expected of his admirers

parts.words: Brand loyalty is expected of his admirers
parts.note: Brand is an 1865 verse play by the Norwegian dramatist, so his fans should be loyal to it

explanation.surface: Fans are expected to stick with a particular product.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brand loyalty' looks like marketing; Brand is the play by Henrik Ibsen.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norwegian dramatist Henrik Ibsen wrote Brand, so his admirers would be loyal to it.

clue.text: A child of five like Doctor Angelicus

parts.note: a quin is one of quintuplets, five children born together
as can mean like, as in 'white as snow'

explanation.surface: A child from a set of five resembles an angelic scholar.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor Angelicus, the Angelic Doctor, is the title of Thomas Aquinas.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas the medieval theologian is known as the Angelic Doctor, in Latin Doctor Angelicus.

clue.text: Bromfield recorded their arrival

parts.note: Louis Bromfield's 1937 novel set in India is titled The ___ Came, about the monsoon

explanation.surface: Someone called Bromfield noted when certain people arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: Louis Bromfield's novel is The Rains Came.
explanation.definitionFit: Monsoon downpours, whose coming gives Louis Bromfield's novel its title.

clue.text: Revise meaning to reveal essayist

indicators.note: revise means rework or alter, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Rewrite the sense to show who wrote the essays.
explanation.definitionFit: The French Renaissance writer Michel de Montaigne invented the essay as a literary form.

clue.text: Collins offers extract from Georges Jacques Danton in a different setting

indicators.note: extract means a passage taken out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Collins quotes a passage about the French revolutionary Danton placed in another setting.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilkie Collins's first novel, set in Rome under Gothic siege, is Antonina; 'in a different setting' adds the surface that the letters sit in other words.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilkie Collins's 1850 historical novel, set in fifth-century Rome, bears this title.

clue.text: Plot is complicated by Shakespearean ensign

indicators.note: complicated means tangled, so the letters of the words before it are mixed up

explanation.surface: A plot made intricate by a Shakespeare character.
explanation.definitionFit: Falstaff's swaggering companion, ensign or 'ancient' in Henry V and Henry IV Part 2.
